knowledge_type_note: A method with a clear precondition — the pawns being advanced must not be your own king's shelter.

history.notes: Standard vocabulary; no coinage researched. The systematic treatment of opposite-side-castling races is attributable to the modern attacking literature rather than to any individual.

engine_era_note: Engines storm readily with opposite-side castling and are notably reluctant to do so with same-side castling, which matches the precondition exactly. They also find the central counter-blow far faster than humans do, which has made premature storms harder to get away with.

preconditions: A group of pawns advancing towards the enemy king
Pieces available to use the lines that open
indicators_for: Opposite-side castling, so the storming pawns are not your own shelter
A hook — an advanced enemy shield pawn to attack
The centre is closed or under control
Rooks already placed on the files that will open
indicators_against: Same-side castling, so the storm exposes your own king
The centre is open or can be opened by the defender
No pieces can follow into the opened lines
The defender is faster in the race
false_positive_traps: Advancing pawns at a king is not an attack unless pieces can follow. Without that, it is a structural concession.
With same-side castling the same moves that attack also expose, and this is the commonest way a storm rebounds.
Counting the storm's speed without counting the defender's central break is how these positions are misjudged.

typical_plans: Count tempi to contact and start first
Attack a hook to force a file open
Combine the storm with prophylaxis against the counter-attack
typical_pawn_structures: Opposite-side castling with pawn masses facing each other
A defender's h6 or g6 as a hook
tactical_consequences: Sacrifices to open the last file are routine and often correct
strategic_consequences: A failed storm usually leaves the attacker structurally worse for the endgame

exceptions: With same-side castling the storm is a concession first and an attack second.
A central counter-blow refutes a premature storm — the standard antidote.
Against an intact shield with no hook, the storm may never force a file open at all.
limitations: Whether the storm arrives first is a concrete calculation, not a judgement.
misconceptions: That pushing pawns at the king is an attack. It is a way of making a road; without pieces it is a weakness.
That storms are always double-edged. With opposite-side castling they cost the attacker nothing.

conflicts.resolution: The same pawn moves attack and expose, and the resolution is which king they shelter. Opposite-side castling removes the conflict entirely; same-side castling makes it acute, and there king safety wins unless a concrete line says otherwise.

by_level.beginner: Push your pawns at their king to open a line your rooks and queen can use.
by_level.intermediate: A pawn storm. It is nearly free when you have castled on the opposite side, and expensive when you have castled on the same side.
by_level.advanced: The pawns make the road; the pieces do the work. Look for a hook to attack, and check the centre before committing.
by_level.master: In opposite-castling races count tempi to contact, and combine the storm with prophylaxis rather than racing blind.

by_depth.short: Push pawns at their king to open a file.
by_depth.normal: A pawn storm: advancing pawns at the enemy king to trade off its shelter and open a line for your pieces. It costs nothing when you have castled on the other wing, and dismantles your own cover when you have not.
by_depth.deep: The pawns are the tool, not the attack — their job is to force a file open for the pieces behind them. The precondition is whose shelter they are: with opposite-side castling they are not yours, so the game becomes a race where one tempo decides; with same-side castling the same advance exposes you. A hook makes it work, since an advanced enemy shield pawn gives you something to attack; against an intact shield the file usually has to be forced with a sacrifice. The standard refutation is a central counter-blow, since a wing attack is only as sound as your control of the centre.

explanations.lesson: Before storming, ask two questions: are these pawns sheltering my own king, and can my pieces follow into the lines that open?

beginner_words: push the pawns at their king

definition_short: Advancing a group of pawns at the enemy king to open a file for the pieces behind them.
definition_long:
Pawns are a barrier, and the king is safe behind them; a storm's purpose is to trade that barrier away and open a line the heavy pieces can use. The pawns are not the attack — they are the tool that creates the road.

THE PRECONDITION is which pawns you are pushing. With OPPOSITE-SIDE CASTLING the g- and h-pawns are not your own king's shelter, so they can be thrown forward at no cost to your own safety, and the game becomes a race in which a single tempo decides. With SAME-SIDE CASTLING the same advance dismantles your own cover, and the burden of proof shifts entirely onto the attacker.

A HOOK makes it work. If the defender has advanced a shield pawn — ...h6, say — the attacker has something to attack with g4-g5, which forces the file open. Against an intact f7-g7-h7 there is nothing to bite on, and the storm has to force the exchange itself, usually with a sacrifice.

The standard refutation is a central counter-blow: a wing attack is only as sound as your control of the centre, and the classic punishment for a premature storm is ...d5 opening lines at the storming side's own king.
